claim: C. elegans embryonic elongation involves a four-fold increase in length without cell migration, cell division, or a notable change in embryonic volume.
source: During its elongation, the embryo evolves from a lima-bean shape to a typical cylindrical shape with a four-fold increase in length, without cell migration, cell division, or a notable change in embryonic volume (Sulston et al., 1983; Priess and Hirsh, 1986) (Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Sulston et al., 1983; Priess and Hirsh, 1986) and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Embryonic elongation requires the epidermal actomyosin cytoskeleton, which acts mostly in the lateral epidermis (seam cells).
source: This process requires the epidermal actomyosin cytoskeleton, which acts mostly in the lateral epidermis (also called seam cells), while the dorso-ventral (DV) epidermal cells may remain passive (Appendix 1) (Wissmann et al., 1997; 1999; Shelton et al., 1999; Piekny et al., 2003; Diogon et al., 2007; Gally et al., 2009; Chan et al., 2015; Vuong-Brender et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work and reference to Appendix 1.

claim: Non-muscle myosin II is concentrated in seam cells.
source: Indeed, the non-muscle myosin II is concentrated in seam cells; in addition, short disorganized actin filaments, which favour actomyosin contractility, are present in seam cells but not in the DV epidermis, where they instead form parallel circumferential bundles (Figure 1b–d) (Gally et al., 2009; Priess and Hirsh, 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Gally et al., 2009; Priess and Hirsh, 1986) and reference to Figure 1b-d.

claim: Short disorganized actin filaments are present in seam cells but not in the DV epidermis, where they instead form parallel circumferential bundles.
source: Indeed, the non-muscle myosin II is concentrated in seam cells; in addition, short disorganized actin filaments, which favour actomyosin contractility, are present in seam cells but not in the DV epidermis, where they instead form parallel circumferential bundles (Figure 1b–d) (Gally et al., 2009; Priess and Hirsh, 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Gally et al., 2009; Priess and Hirsh, 1986) and reference to Figure 1b-d.

claim: Actomyosin forces are thought to squeeze the embryo circumferentially, thereby increasing the hydrostatic pressure and promoting embryo elongation in the antero-posterior direction.
source: The actomyosin forces are thought to squeeze the embryo circumferentially, thereby increasing the hydrostatic pressure and promoting embryo elongation in the antero-posterior (AP) direction (Priess and Hirsh, 1986) (Figure 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Priess and Hirsh, 1986) and reference to Figure 1e.

claim: Myosin II does not show a polarized distribution in C. elegans embryonic epidermis.
source: First, myosin II does not show a polarized distribution (Figure 1f,g), nor does it display dynamic pulsatile foci at this stage; hence, it is difficult to account for the circumferential squeezing.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1f,g showing myosin II distribution.

claim: Myosin II does not display dynamic pulsatile foci during early C. elegans embryonic elongation.
source: First, myosin II does not show a polarized distribution (Figure 1f,g), nor does it display dynamic pulsatile foci at this stage; hence, it is difficult to account for the circumferential squeezing.
evidence: The claim is based on observations at the stage being studied.

claim: The opening hole within the actin cytoskeleton after laser ablation reached equilibrium in less than 10 s in more than 80% of cases.
source: In the first (accounting for >80% of the cases), the opening hole within the actin cytoskeleton reached equilibrium in less than 10 s, and resealed within less than 2 min (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Video 1.

claim: The opening hole within the actin cytoskeleton after laser ablation resealed within less than 2 min in more than 80% of cases.
source: In the first (accounting for >80% of the cases), the opening hole within the actin cytoskeleton reached equilibrium in less than 10 s, and resealed within less than 2 min (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Video 1.

claim: The opening in the seam cell H1 at the 1.5F stage in let-502(sb118ts) embryos was significantly smaller than that in WT embryos.
source: As shown in Figure 2c, the opening in the seam cell H1 at the 1.5F stage in let-502(sb118ts) embryos changed very little and was significantly smaller than that in WT embryos, consistent with a decrease in mechanical stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The reduced opening in let-502(sb118ts) embryos is consistent with a decrease in mechanical stress.
source: As shown in Figure 2c, the opening in the seam cell H1 at the 1.5F stage in let-502(sb118ts) embryos changed very little and was significantly smaller than that in WT embryos, consistent with a decrease in mechanical stress.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing reduced opening in let-502 mutants.

claim: At the 1.3F stage in H1, there was no significant stress anisotropy.
source: At the 1.3F stage in H1, there was no significant stress anisotropy; however, as the embryo elongated to the 1.5F and 1.7F stages, the stress became anisotropic (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: As the embryo elongated to the 1.5F and 1.7F stages, the stress in H1 became anisotropic.
source: At the 1.3F stage in H1, there was no significant stress anisotropy; however, as the embryo elongated to the 1.5F and 1.7F stages, the stress became anisotropic (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: In V3, the anisotropy of stress evolved in the opposite direction compared to H1, with higher stress anisotropy at the 1.3F stage compared to the 1.5F stage.
source: In V3, the anisotropy of stress evolved in the opposite direction, with higher stress anisotropy at the 1.3F stage compared to the 1.5F stage (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: In V6, the stress was slightly anisotropic at both the 1.3F and the 1.5F stage.
source: In V6, the stress was slightly anisotropic at both the 1.3F and the 1.5F stage (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Whenever the stress became anisotropic in seam cells, it was higher in the DV direction.
source: In all cells, whenever the stress became anisotropic, it was higher in the DV direction.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations across multiple cells.

claim: The head diameter did not diminish between the 1.3F and 1.5F stages when the stress was nearly isotropic.
source: The head diameter did not diminish between the 1.3F and 1.5F stages when the stress was nearly isotropic, but decreased significantly between the 1.5F and 1.7F stages as the stress anisotropy increased.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological measurements and correlation with stress data.

claim: The head diameter decreased significantly between the 1.5F and 1.7F stages as the stress anisotropy increased.
source: The head diameter did not diminish between the 1.3F and 1.5F stages when the stress was nearly isotropic, but decreased significantly between the 1.5F and 1.7F stages as the stress anisotropy increased.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological measurements and correlation with stress data.

claim: The body diameter decreased most rapidly between the 1.3F and 1.5F stages, when the stress was highly anisotropic.
source: Conversely, the body diameter decreased most rapidly between the 1.3F and 1.5F stages, when the stress was highly anisotropic, then changed at a lower pace beyond the 1.5F stage, when the stress became less anisotropic.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological measurements and correlation with stress data.

claim: The local morphological changes within the embryo correlate with locally higher stress in the DV compared to the AP direction.
source: Thus, the local morphological changes within the embryo correlate with locally higher stress in the DV compared to the AP direction.
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis between morphological changes and stress measurements.

claim: At the level of V3, the decrease in body diameter came from both seam (V3) and DV cells.
source: At the level of V3, the decrease in body diameter came from both seam (V3) and DV cells, whereas in the head, it came mainly from DV cells (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of cell width shown in Figure 3e.

claim: In the head, the decrease in diameter came mainly from DV cells.
source: At the level of V3, the decrease in body diameter came from both seam (V3) and DV cells, whereas in the head, it came mainly from DV cells (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of cell width shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Both seam and DV epidermal cells contribute to the changes in embryo diameter, irrespective of their level of active myosin II.
source: Furthermore, we found that both seam and DV epidermal cells contribute to the changes in embryo diameter, irrespective of their level of active myosin II.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of cell width changes.

claim: In spc-1(RNAi) embryos at a developmental timing equivalent to the 1.7F stage, there was a smaller opening in both AP and DV directions compared to WT.
source: In spc-1(RNAi) embryos, at a developmental timing equivalent to the 1.7F stage in control embryos, we found a smaller opening in both AP and DV directions and a decrease of AS compared to WT (Figure 3f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f,g.

claim: In spc-1(RNAi) embryos at a developmental timing equivalent to the 1.7F stage, there was a decrease of AS compared to WT.
source: In spc-1(RNAi) embryos, at a developmental timing equivalent to the 1.7F stage in control embryos, we found a smaller opening in both AP and DV directions and a decrease of AS compared to WT (Figure 3f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f,g.

claim: The reduced opening and AS in spc-1(RNAi) embryos may account for their slower elongation rate and arrest at the 2F stage.
source: This may account for the slower elongation rate of spc-1(RNAi) embryos and their arrest at the 2F stage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data correlating mechanical properties with elongation phenotype.

claim: Spectrin partially contributes to the AS at the 1.7F stage.
source: Thus, spectrin partially contributes to the AS at the 1.7F stage.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the spc-1(RNAi) experimental results.

claim: Embryos depleted in UNC-112/Kindlin showed a significantly larger opening in both the AP and DV directions at the 1.7F stage compared to controls.
source: Compared to controls, embryos that are depleted in UNC-112/Kindlin, which mediates sarcomere assembly (Rogalski et al., 2000), showed a significantly larger opening in both the AP and DV directions at the 1.7F stage, but no change in stress anisotropy (Figure 3f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f,g and citation to prior work (Rogalski et al., 2000).

claim: Embryos depleted in UNC-112/Kindlin showed no change in stress anisotropy at the 1.7F stage compared to controls.
source: Compared to controls, embryos that are depleted in UNC-112/Kindlin, which mediates sarcomere assembly (Rogalski et al., 2000), showed a significantly larger opening in both the AP and DV directions at the 1.7F stage, but no change in stress anisotropy (Figure 3f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f,g.

claim: AS establishment in the H1 cell after the 1.5F stage is independent of muscle contractions.
source: Thus, AS establishment in the H1 cell after the 1.5F stage is independent of muscle contractions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the unc-112(RNAi) experimental results showing no change in AS despite muscle defects.

claim: The AS of the head can be determined based on embryo geometry.
source: Thus, the AS of the head can be determined easily.
evidence: The claim is based on the application of thin-wall vessel model to the embryo geometry.

claim: The AS predicted by the thin-wall vessel model is nearly identical to those derived experimentally using laser ablation.
source: Given the head and body diameter of the embryo (Figure 3c), we can compare the AS predicted by the thin-wall vessel model with those derived experimentally using laser ablation (Figure 4g). These values are nearly identical, showing that AS can be predicted on the basis of embryonic geometry.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: AS can be predicted on the basis of embryonic geometry.
source: These values are nearly identical, showing that AS can be predicted on the basis of embryonic geometry.
evidence: The claim is based on the agreement between model predictions and experimental measurements.

claim: The AS induces morphological changes in embryonic seam cells.
source: In conclusion, our experimental and modelling data show that the AS induces morphological changes in embryonic seam cells and provide a basis for understanding how the embryo elongates from a mechanical standpoint.
evidence: The claim is based on combined experimental data and modeling results.

claim: In the HYP7 cell, the opening in the DV direction was larger than that in the AP direction at the 1.5F and 1.7F stages.
source: In the HYP7 cell, the opening in the DV direction was larger than that in the AP direction (Figure 5b; dorsal and ventral cells behaved similarly after laser cutting) at the 1.5F and 1.7F stages, as was the case in the H1 cell (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Dorsal and ventral HYP7 cells behaved similarly after laser cutting.
source: In the HYP7 cell, the opening in the DV direction was larger than that in the AP direction (Figure 5b; dorsal and ventral cells behaved similarly after laser cutting) at the 1.5F and 1.7F stages, as was the case in the H1 cell (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations during laser ablation experiments.

claim: The ratio of DV/AP opening in HYP7 was greater than that in H1.
source: However, the ratio of DV/AP opening in HYP7 was greater than that in H1 (Figure 5c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The HYP7 cell has anisotropic cortical material properties.
source: Hence, this suggests that the HYP7 cell has anisotropic cortical material properties.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the discrepancy between model predictions for isotropic material and experimental observations.

claim: The Young modulus of the HYP7 matrix without fibers was about 1.5 times stiffer than that of H1.
source: As the DV opening of HYP7 was about 1.5 times smaller than that of H1 (Figure 7a), we infer that the Young modulus of the HYP7 matrix without fibers was about 1.5 times stiffer than that of H1 (Appendix 9), suggesting that these cells have distinct material properties.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 7a and calculations in Appendix 9.

claim: H1 and HYP7 cells have distinct material properties.
source: As the DV opening of HYP7 was about 1.5 times smaller than that of H1 (Figure 7a), we infer that the Young modulus of the HYP7 matrix without fibers was about 1.5 times stiffer than that of H1 (Appendix 9), suggesting that these cells have distinct material properties.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and modeling.

claim: The factor K increased during early elongation in HYP7 cells.
source: Comparing the DV and AP opening for the HYP7 cell, we found that the factor K increased during early elongation (Figure 7b; Appendix 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by calculations shown in Figure 7b and Appendix 10.

claim: The calculated ratio of DV/AP Young moduli in HYP7 increased during early elongation and was greater than the DV/AP stress anisotropy.
source: More importantly, the calculated ratio of DV/AP Young moduli also increased, and was greater than the DV/AP stress anisotropy (Figure 7c).
evidence: The claim is supported by calculations shown in Figure 7c.

claim: When the DV/AP stiffness anisotropy increases and is greater than the DV/AP stress anisotropy, elongation along the AP direction is favored in HYP7 cells.
source: Altogether, our model strongly suggests that when the DV/AP stiffness anisotropy increases and is greater than the DV/AP stress anisotropy, as observed in the head HYP7 (Figure 7c), elongation along the AP direction is favored.
evidence: The claim is based on modeling predictions and experimental observations shown in Figure 7c.

claim: The distinct mechanical properties of the cells composing a complex tissue enables its morphogenesis, which does not require all cells to be contractile.
source: Furthermore, our data demonstrate that the distinct mechanical properties of the cells composing a complex tissue enables its morphogenesis , which does not require all cells to be contractile.
evidence: The claim is based on the overall findings from the study showing that both contractile seam cells and non-contractile DV cells contribute to elongation.

claim: The polarization of actin filaments in seam cells correlated with the observed pattern of stress anisotropy.
source: We found that the polarization of actin filaments in seam cells correlated with the observed pattern of stress anisotropy.
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis between actin alignment measurements and stress anisotropy data.

claim: In H1 at the 1.3F stage, actin filaments had a nearly isotropic angular distribution correlating with the isotropic stress.
source: Indeed, in H1 at the 1.3F stage, actin filaments had a nearly isotropic angular distribution correlating with the isotropic stress (Figure 8a, Figure 3b), whereas they became increasingly aligned along the DV direction from the 1.3F to the 1.7F stage (Figure 8a), mirroring the increasing stress anisotropy from 1.3F to 1.7F (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by actin alignment data shown in Figure 8a and stress data in Figure 3b.

claim: Actin filaments in H1 became increasingly aligned along the DV direction from the 1.3F to the 1.7F stage, mirroring the increasing stress anisotropy.
source: Indeed, in H1 at the 1.3F stage, actin filaments had a nearly isotropic angular distribution correlating with the isotropic stress (Figure 8a, Figure 3b), whereas they became increasingly aligned along the DV direction from the 1.3F to the 1.7F stage (Figure 8a), mirroring the increasing stress anisotropy from 1.3F to 1.7F (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by actin alignment data shown in Figure 8a and stress data in Figure 3b.

claim: Actin alignment decreased along the DV direction in V3 from the 1.3F to the 1.5F stage, in parallel to the decrease of stress anisotropy between those stages.
source: Likewise, actin alignment decreased along the DV direction in V3 from the 1.3F to the 1.5F stage, in parallel to the decrease of stress anisotropy between those stages (Figures 8b and 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by actin alignment data shown in Figure 8b and stress data in Figure 3b.

claim: In the HYP7 cell, actin filaments already acquired a preferential DV alignment at the 1.3F stage.
source: In the HYP7 cell, actin filaments already acquired a preferential DV alignment at the 1.3F stage (Figure 8c), but became increasingly organized along the DV direction as the embryo elongated to the 2F stage, with a highly significant difference between the 1.5F and 1.7F stages (Figure 8c and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by actin alignment data shown in Figure 8c.

claim: Actin filaments in HYP7 became increasingly organized along the DV direction as the embryo elongated to the 2F stage, with a highly significant difference between the 1.5F and 1.7F stages.
source: In the HYP7 cell, actin filaments already acquired a preferential DV alignment at the 1.3F stage (Figure 8c), but became increasingly organized along the DV direction as the embryo elongated to the 2F stage, with a highly significant difference between the 1.5F and 1.7F stages (Figure 8c and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by actin alignment data shown in Figure 8c and f.

claim: Changes in actin alignment in HYP7 correlated with the increased stiffness anisotropy observed in the HYP7 cell.
source: These changes correlated with the increased stiffness anisotropy observed in the HYP7 cell (Figure 7c).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation between actin alignment data and stiffness anisotropy calculations shown in Figure 7c.

claim: The pattern of actin distribution showed a good correlation with the observed stress and stiffness anisotropy.
source: Altogether, we conclude that the pattern of actin distribution showed a good correlation with the observed stress and stiffness anisotropy.
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis between actin alignment and mechanical properties.

claim: C. elegans embryonic elongation does not involve myosin-II-polarized distribution nor actomyosin pulses.
source: The C. elegans embryonic elongation is distinct from those situations because it does not involve myosin-II-polarized distribution nor actomyosin pulses.
evidence: The claim is based on observations of myosin II distribution and dynamics in the study.

claim: C. elegans embryonic elongation still requires stress anisotropy despite not having myosin-II-polarized distribution or actomyosin pulses.
source: Interestingly, this process still requires stress anisotropy, outlining that stress anisotropy can be produced by different means.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental findings showing stress anisotropy is important for elongation.

claim: Stress anisotropy can be produced by different means.
source: Interestingly, this process still requires stress anisotropy, outlining that stress anisotropy can be produced by different means.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing C. elegans with other systems.

claim: Myosin II activity displays an asymmetric distribution along the embryo circumference in cells with different material properties.
source: Second, akin to a planar polarized distribution, myosin II activity displays an asymmetric distribution along the embryo circumference in cells with different material properties (Figure 8g).
evidence: The claim is based on observations of myosin II distribution and reference to Figure 8g.

claim: The spectrin cytoskeleton has a significant role in establishing normal levels of stress magnitude and anisotropy.
source: Third, we found that the spectrin cytoskeleton has a significant role in establishing normal levels of stress magnitude and anisotropy.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental results from spc-1(RNAi) embryos.

claim: Spectrin is known to impinge on actin filament alignment and continuity in DV cells.
source: Spectrin is known to impinge on actin filament alignment and continuity in DV cells (Praitis et al., 2005; Norman and Moerman, 2002) and could thus affect DV stiffness anisotropy by reducing the level of actin fiber alignment.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Praitis et al., 2005; Norman and Moerman, 2002).

claim: Spectrin could affect DV stiffness anisotropy by reducing the level of actin fiber alignment.
source: Spectrin is known to impinge on actin filament alignment and continuity in DV cells (Praitis et al., 2005; Norman and Moerman, 2002) and could thus affect DV stiffness anisotropy by reducing the level of actin fiber alignment.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the mechanism by which spectrin affects stiffness.

claim: The juxtaposition of cells with different 'physical phenotypes', seam epidermis expressing stress anisotropy and DV epidermal cell showing stiffness anisotropy, powers C. elegans elongation.
source: Thus, the juxtaposition of cells with different 'physical phenotypes', seam epidermis expressing stress anisotropy and DV epidermal cell showing stiffness anisotropy, powers C. elegans elongation, as previously suggested in chicken limb bud outgrowth (Damon et al., 2008) or chick intestinal looping (Savin et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on the overall findings of the study and comparison with other systems cited (Damon et al., 2008; Savin et al., 2011).

claim: Tissue elongation relies on two fundamental physical quantities: mechanical stress and tissue stiffness.
source: In conclusion, our work shows that tissue elongation relies on two fundamental physical quantities (mechanical stress and tissue stiffness), and provides the most advanced mesoscopic understanding to date of the mechanics at work during the first steps of C. elegans embryonic elongation.
evidence: The claim is based on the overall findings and conclusions of the study.

claim: The work provides the most advanced mesoscopic understanding to date of the mechanics at work during the first steps of C. elegans embryonic elongation.
source: In conclusion, our work shows that tissue elongation relies on two fundamental physical quantities (mechanical stress and tissue stiffness), and provides the most advanced mesoscopic understanding to date of the mechanics at work during the first steps of C. elegans embryonic elongation.
evidence: The claim is an assessment of the contribution of the work based on the comprehensive analysis performed.

claim: Actin filaments progressively organize into circumferential parallel bundles in DV cells during embryonic elongation.
source: Actin filaments progressively organize into circumferential parallel bundles in DV cells (arrows), arrowheads point to seam cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1b-d.

claim: The integrated ABD::GFP marker shows some cell to cell variation in expression.
source: Note that the integrated ABD::GFP marker shows some cell to cell variation in expression.
evidence: The claim is based on observations of the marker expression.

claim: The minor to major axis ratio of the opening ellipse is independent of the initial cut length when the cut length varied from 3 μm to 6 μm.
source: We found that it is the case when the cut length varied from 3 μm to 6 μm (Appendix 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental validation described in Appendix 4.

claim: The half-time of the cut border relaxation was similar in the AP and DV directions.
source: The half-time of the cut border relaxation, which depends on the ratio of viscosity over stiffness, was similar in the AP and DV directions (Appendix 3), supporting the hypothesis that the seam cell cortex is isotropic.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis described in Appendix 3.

claim: The seam cell cortex is isotropic.
source: The half-time of the cut border relaxation, which depends on the ratio of viscosity over stiffness, was similar in the AP and DV directions (Appendix 3), supporting the hypothesis that the seam cell cortex is isotropic.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the relaxation half-time data.

claim: There was an agreement between methods based on equilibrium shape and recoil dynamics for the AP versus DV stress ratio.
source: We found an agreement between both methods for the AP versus DV stress ratio, and similar trends for the stress magnitude.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of different analysis methods described in Appendix 3.

claim: Embryos showing the first type of ablation response (local cortex disruption) continued to develop and hatched.
source: Embryos showing the first response continued to develop and hatched, whereas those showing the second response arrested their development and eventually died.
evidence: The claim is based on observations of embryo development after ablation.

claim: Embryos showing the second type of ablation response (wounding response) arrested their development and eventually died.
source: Embryos showing the first response continued to develop and hatched, whereas those showing the second response arrested their development and eventually died.
evidence: The claim is based on observations of embryo development after ablation.

claim: The head, body and tail diameter decreased at different rates over time during embryonic elongation.
source: We observed that the head, body and tail diameter (at the levels of H1, V3 and V6, respectively) decreased at different rates over time (Figure 3c), as also observed by Martin and colleagues (Martin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological measurements shown in Figure 3c and citation to prior work (Martin et al., 2014).

claim: The tail diameter decreased nearly linearly between the 1.3F and 1.7F stages, at a lower rate than the body diameter.
source: Finally, the tail diameter decreased nearly linearly between the 1.3F and 1.7F stages, at a lower rate than the body diameter, coinciding with a smaller anisotropic stress in V6.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological measurements and correlation with stress data.

claim: The decrease in tail diameter coincided with a smaller anisotropic stress in V6.
source: Finally, the tail diameter decreased nearly linearly between the 1.3F and 1.7F stages, at a lower rate than the body diameter, coinciding with a smaller anisotropic stress in V6.
evidence: The claim is based on correlation between morphological changes and stress measurements.

claim: UNC-112/Kindlin mediates sarcomere assembly.
source: Compared to controls, embryos that are depleted in UNC-112/Kindlin, which mediates sarcomere assembly (Rogalski et al., 2000), showed a significantly larger opening in both the AP and DV directions at the 1.7F stage, but no change in stress anisotropy (Figure 3f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Rogalski et al., 2000).

claim: unc-112(RNAi) embryos elongate up to 1.7F similarly to WT.
source: This is consistent with their wild-type elongation rate up to the 2F stage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by elongation measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The C. elegans embryo can be modeled as an isotropic thin-wall vessel with capped ends under hydrostatic pressure.
source: We can thus model the C. elegans embryo as an isotropic thin-wall (the epidermis) vessel with capped ends under hydrostatic pressure, and can determine the relationship between the mechanical stress on the epidermis and the embryo shape.
evidence: The claim is based on the application of physical modeling principles to the embryo geometry.

claim: The AS factor is equal to one for a sphere.
source: Typically, the AS factor, or the DV to AP stress ratio, is equal to one for a sphere, equal to two for a cylinder and takes an intermediate value between 1 and 2 for an ellipsoid.
evidence: The claim is based on established physical principles for thin-wall vessels.

claim: The AS factor is equal to two for a cylinder.
source: Typically, the AS factor, or the DV to AP stress ratio, is equal to one for a sphere, equal to two for a cylinder and takes an intermediate value between 1 and 2 for an ellipsoid.
evidence: The claim is based on established physical principles for thin-wall vessels.

claim: The AS factor takes an intermediate value between 1 and 2 for an ellipsoid.
source: Typically, the AS factor, or the DV to AP stress ratio, is equal to one for a sphere, equal to two for a cylinder and takes an intermediate value between 1 and 2 for an ellipsoid.
evidence: The claim is based on established physical principles for thin-wall vessels.

claim: The AP stress among the seam cells at a given stage differs by 20%.
source: We previously observed that the AP stress among the seam cells at a given stage differs by 20% (Figure 3b).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The head evolves from a sphere to an ellipsoid between the 1.5F to the 1.7F stages as the AS becomes greater than 1.
source: Indeed, consistent with the equations, the head evolves from a sphere to an ellipsoid between the 1.5F to the 1.7F stages as the AS becomes greater than 1 (Figure 3b,c).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological observations and stress measurements shown in Figure 3b,c.

claim: The seam cell dimension increases along the AP axis with the AS.
source: The resulting equations, which assume that seam cells have an isotropic cortex and are subjected to contractile stress, correctly predict that the seam cell dimension increases along the AP axis (εAP) with the AS (Figure 4h–j), and decreases along the DV axis (εDV).
evidence: The claim is based on modeling predictions shown in Figure 4h-j.

claim: The seam cell dimension decreases along the DV axis with the AS.
source: The resulting equations, which assume that seam cells have an isotropic cortex and are subjected to contractile stress, correctly predict that the seam cell dimension increases along the AP axis (εAP) with the AS (Figure 4h–j), and decreases along the DV axis (εDV).
evidence: The claim is based on modeling predictions shown in Figure 4h-j.

claim: The RhoGAP RGA-2 maintains myosin II activation in DV cells at a low level.
source: As the RhoGAP RGA-2 maintains myosin II activation in these cells at a low level (Diogon et al., 2007), actomyosin contractility in DV cells cannot account for such changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Diogon et al., 2007).

claim: Actomyosin contractility in DV cells cannot account for the head diameter reduction.
source: As the RhoGAP RGA-2 maintains myosin II activation in these cells at a low level (Diogon et al., 2007), actomyosin contractility in DV cells cannot account for such changes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the low myosin II activity in DV cells.

claim: Polarized actin distribution could affect cell stiffness based on recent observations.
source: However, in contrast to seam cells, DV epidermal cells have circumferentially oriented actin bundles (Figure 1b–d), which based on recent observation could affect cell stiffness (Calzado-Martín et al., 2016; Salker et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent work (Calzado-Martín et al., 2016; Salker et al., 2016).

claim: The circumferential polarized actin distribution in DV epidermal cells could induce greater stiffness in that direction and thereby influences their deformation.
source: We thus hypothesized that the circumferential polarized actin distribution in DV epidermal cells could induce greater stiffness in that direction and thereby influences their deformation.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observation of actin organization and knowledge from other systems.

claim: The orthotropic model did not adequately describe the laser-cutting data from the DV epidermis.
